learning.title: A hardcoded identity literal is a fact about the world, not a floor: the discriminator is where the new value came from
learning.trigger: A gate test hardcodes a value the product is licensed to change - a source digest, a revision prefix, a pinned identity - and the change under review moves it. Typical shape: `assert.equal(identity.digest, "<64 hex>")`, or a fixture that spreads the real baseline (`{...baseline}`) and therefore silently inherits an identity that no longer describes it.
learning.mistake: Two opposite errors wear the same clothes. Treating the literal as a floor ("never edit a test") leaves the suite red on a lawful change, which pressure then resolves by weakening something real. Treating every red as a stale literal lets a genuine mismatch become a new constant, which is suppression. The PR that first landed a UX-ruling refresh (248#6942308107) sat on the wrong side of this: three tests in `paper-source-profiles.node.mjs` and one in `paper-whole-artboard.node.mjs` pinned the auth source's V-0 digest `a6978501` and assumed `source.revision` reads `paper:...`, while a ruling refresh replaces `source` wholesale with `ux-ruling:<issue>#<comment>; app:<sha>`. Two of the fixtures were not even about the literal: they spread the live baseline and deleted `sourceProfiles`, so they inherited the ruling identity and then exercised a V-0 path against it.
learning.rule: Ask where the new value came from before touching the test. If it is derived by the shipped path the change is exercising - recomputed by the production function, or produced by the shipped writer - then the old literal is a stale description of the world and updating it is a correction; the assertions' shapes must survive untouched, and `git log -S "<old literal>"` is the evidence that the literal is a snapshot rather than a guard (unchanged since release proves no lawful refresh had ever landed). If the new value came from the failure itself - pasted out of the assertion diff, or produced only by editing an input list, a floor or the comparison - it is suppression, and the answer is to fix the cause. Fixtures that spread the real baseline (`{...baseline}`) are the trap: a wholesale identity replacement silently changes what they test, so a fixture for a legacy path must set that path's identity explicitly rather than inherit the live one. Record the distinction in the PR's Decisions, and make the gate-bug fix its own commit so a reviewer can see it apart from the repin.

verification.requirement: The updated tests assert the same properties as before, with only expected identity values and fixture sources changed; the production function under test is unchanged by the test edit; and the gate that would have refused the lawful change is fixed in a separate commit naming its cause.
